messages.body_plain:
If you're happy with propagating the mean (or an estimate), this sounds
fine. If you want to propatate the whole uncertainty, its a little more
complicated, as, f.exe

1[y=0] * p + (1-p) * f(y)

or f(y|y>0) in the second one. So you see that the prediction involves
also the hyperparameter 'p' and the linear predictor that goes into
f(y). In the case where you have another binary process replacing the
'p', its the same, and you also get this interaction between 1-p and the
fitted values  for f(y).

unless you're happy with the first option above, you have to, I believe,
using inla.posterior.sample() and inla.posterior.sample.eval() to do MC
for predictions and extract their posteriors.

H

On Sun, 2020-05-24 at 18:38 -0700, Mark wrote:
> Hello Håvard,
>
> I solved my issue! However, it would be nice to have a more elegant
> solution. More on that below.
>
> My goal is to fit a hurdle model and predict. My oversight was that
> when I fit a hurdle model with inla.stack, I actually didn’t know what
> I was pulling out of them (I thought I did). But as noted, here is one
> way to solve my issue. Assume we have fit a hurdle model. Then:
>
> ==============================================
>
> # Calculate linear predictor manually, take the inverse link (invlog,
> exp respectively)
>
> INLA_phi_fit<-(design_mat%*%INLA_binomial_coeffs)%>%invlogit
>
> INLA_lambda_fit<-(design_mat%*%INLA_truc_poisson_coeffs)%>%exp
>
> # For zero truncated poisson, the mean is not lambda as in a poisson,
> but lambda/(1-exp(-lambda)):
>
> INLA_trunc_poisson<- INLA_lambda_fit /(1-exp(-INLA_lambda_fit))
>
> # Now, calculate an approximate prediction. Since the binomial and
> truncated poisson parts may be #related, it is not strictly correct to
> do this, but I plan on using these values as approximations.
>
> INLA_manual_preds<-(INLA_logistic*INLA_trunc_poisson)
>
> ==============================================
>
> The above gives virtually identical results to PSCL, which makes sense
> given the weakly informative default priors and lack of any random
> effects in the INLA model I was comparing it with. They are not
> exactly identical because of tiny differences in the estimation of the
> coefficients due to different optimization methods, I assume. But the
> results are very clearly matching even out to the thousandths decimal
> places, unlike before.
>
> However, I don’t know how to get these predictions *directly* from the
> model. In order to make a simple reproducible example of the type of
> model I am working with, I took the hurdle model example from the
> documentation (
> https://inla.r-inla-download.org/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/zeroinflated.pdf
> , page 9), and created the same model, but using inla.stack to match
> how I’m approaching the problem. As you can see, they provide
> identical fits. I fed it dummy A matrices, etc, because I eventually
> want to make it a spatial model eventually and to avoid to error-prone
> matrix manipulation of the example in the documentation.
>
> To summarize: I’m looking to get the hurdle predictions from the model
> output itself rather than doing it manually, but it’s not clear to me
> how to do that. Part of me thinks it is not feasible, because I assume
> that inla.stack is creating the same sort of “checkered” dataset as in
> the example from the documentation on page 9. In this sense, only
> covariates for the binomial or (in the exclusive sense) poisson part
> are available for any given observation in the documentation example.
> Whereas in my pseudo code above that produces correct results, we use
> the design matrix twice, as does PSCL. Any thoughts on how to do that
> are welcome!
>
> Regards,
>
> Mark
>
>

If you by sqrt you mean

Q=AA

With symmetric A, Like using the sqrt of the eigenvalue and the eigenvector matrix, then no.

If you by sqrt mean

Q=AA’

Then yes, if A is lower-triangular, then this is just the Cholesky factorisation.

Hi all,

I am fitting a preferential model and so I have to have one stack for the marks likelihood and another for the point process and I want to make predictions of  the marks and of the latent field. However, when I tried to combine the four stacks I had this error

> Error in (function (...)  : Name mismatch.

I discovered that the error occur when I add the stack for the prediction of the marks (stack.pr <http://stack.pr>). Below are my stacks.

stack.obs<-inla.stack(data=list(y=cbind(y,NA),e=rep(0,n)),
                      A=list(obs,1),
                      effects=list(spatial.field=s.index$spatial.field,
                                   list(data.frame(b0.y=rep(1,n)))),
                      tag="response")
stack.pp<-inla.stack(data=list(y=cbind(NA,ypp),e=epp),
                     A=list(App,1),
                     effects=list(i=s.index$spatial.field,
                                  list(data.frame(b0.pp=rep(1,nv+n),depth=depth.point))),
                     tag="pp")
stack.pr <http://stack.pr><-inla.stack(data=list(y=NA),
                   A=list(Ap),
                   effects=list(c(s.index,list(b0.y=1))),
                   tag="pred.response")
stack.pred<-inla.stack(data=list(xi=NA),
                       A=list(Ap),
                       effects=list(s.index),
                       tag="pred.latent")

join.stack<-inla.stack(stack.obs,stack.pp,stack.pr <http://stack.pr>,stack.pred)

Can anyone help me?

Thanks in advance,
Lídia

messages.subject: How are constraints handled under the hood in INLA?
messages.subject_clean: How are constraints handled under the hood in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA-users,

I am wondering how constraints are handled internally in INLA (NOT how to  specify them in the software), more specifically a sum to zero constraint on the besag model (intrinsic Gaussian markov random field, where you add a constant to the diagonal to make it SPD.  Rank deficiency 1)

It is unclear to me how INLA calculates the log likelihood of this density in the calculations performed (or does INLA do something else?)

I have  made some observations below:

>From the note "Approximate inference for Hierarchical Gaussian Markov Random Fields Models" by Rue and Martino, on p. 8: "Since linear constraints destroy the sparseness of the precision matrix it will not allow for fast computation of the marginal variances."  A formula is used to correct the marignal variances.

To sample from such a field it seems like conditioning  by Kriging can be used, see Eq 2.30 in Rue's book Gaussian Markov Random Fields

One can also use algorithm 3.1 in the same book to obtain a sample from this distribution.

There is an expression for the likelihood, see Eq 2.31, but the expression is only valid for x such that Ax=e is true. In my case A=[1,1,1,1], e=0. How to handle this constraint with log likelihood?

The software seems to be fast with the constraint, so something clever is done

Thanks,

Fredrik

messages.subject: Modifying an INLA formula so it will work with inlabru, in order to use lime package
messages.subject_clean: Modifying an INLA formula so it will work with inlabru, in order to use lime package
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I used INLA recently to run this model :

bym2a.final16 <- inla(Y ~ X1 : X2 + f(struct, model = "besag", graph = "ADA.coop.train",  scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE, hyper = hyper3) + f(unstruct, model = "iid", hyper = hyper3),
                      data = as.data.frame(ADA.total.pol), family = "poisson", E = tot.offset,
                      control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1))

 Where Y and X1 are numeric variables and X2 is a factor variable. tot.offset is another variable in my dataframe that represents the expected number of cases for each observation. struct and unstruct are just dummy variables I used for the spatial and random effects (1:length(ADA.total.pol).
Everything worked perfectly.

Now, I would like to use the lime package. But the lime package needs a predict function in order to work

In order to have lime support for your model of choice lime needs to be able to get predictions from the model in a standardised way, and it needs to be able to know whether it is a classification or regression model. For the former it calls the predict_model() generic which the user is free to supply methods for without overriding the standard predict() method. For the latter the model must respond to the model_type() generic.

Out of the box, lime supports the following model objects:

train from caret

WrappedModel from mlr

xgb.Booster from xgboost

H2OModel from h2o

keras.engine.training.Model from keras

lda from MASS (used for low-dependency examples)

If your model is not one of the above you'll need to implement support yourself. If the model has a predict interface mimicking that of predict.train() from caret, it will be enough to wrap your model in as_classifier() <https://rstudiodev1.cgic.ca:8787/s/df10ecfc78a31f40afc27/help/library/lime/help/as_classifier>/as_regressor() <https://rstudiodev1.cgic.ca:8787/s/df10ecfc78a31f40afc27/help/library/lime/help/as_regressor> to gain support. Otherwise you'll need need to implement a predict_model() method and potentially a model_type() method (if the latter is omitted the model should be wrapped in as_classifier() <https://rstudiodev1.cgic.ca:8787/s/df10ecfc78a31f40afc27/help/library/lime/help/as_classifier>/as_regressor() <https://rstudiodev1.cgic.ca:8787/s/df10ecfc78a31f40afc27/help/library/lime/help/as_regressor>, everytime it is used in lime() <https://rstudiodev1.cgic.ca:8787/s/df10ecfc78a31f40afc27/help/library/lime/help/lime>).

I thus thought that by refitting my model with inlabru, I could use the lime package since inlabru has a predict function.

However, I am not sure how to convert my INLA formula to an inlabru formula.

I have tried :

b.options <- bru.options(E = ADA.total.pol$tot.offset, result = bym2a.final16)

n_loc <- max(ADA.total.pol$unstruct, na.rm = TRUE)

inla.bru <- bru(Y ~ X1 : X2 + struct(struct, model = "besag", graph = "ADA.coop.train",  scale.model = TRUE) +

                  unstruct(unstruct, model = "iid", n = n_loc),

                data = as.data.frame(ADA.total.pol), family = "poisson", options = b.options)

But I get an error :

Error in `[[<-`(`*tmp*`, ge$f$label, value = smod) :
  no such index at level 1
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In if (label == "offset") { :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used
2: In if (smod$label == "offset") lbl[[k]] = "offset(offset)" :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used

Could someone help me get my inlabru formula right ? Or another way to get the lime package to work with my INLA model ?

Thanks a lot,

Anik

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
can you clarify if this version of the model does run in regular INLA?
We haven't really tested graph based models in inlabru, so there are
likely to be undiscovered problems, so make sure the plain INLA
version is ok first.
Typically, the current version of inla needs an explicit n=... setting
for the model so it can know the number of graph nodes (as it doesn't
know about graphs, and should just pass the graph itself on to inla().

Finn

                      data = as.data.frame(ADA.train.pol3), family = "poisson", E = tot.offset,

Error in Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = seq_len(N), j = idx, x = rep(1, N),  :

Thank you so much for your help,

Anik

Dear Professor Rue and R-INLA groups,

I have run different survival models survival models using R-INLA and faced the following errors

1. The coxPH model has not given the output (it stopped generating the results after some iteration)
2. In the Weibull parametric model, I got the Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed(). In fact, I have included the verbose=TRUE as well.

Kindly see the code below and let you suggest to me what to do.

formula=inla.surv(mydata$time,mydata$Status)~Region+Residence+Mother_education+Source_of_water+Family_size+Toilet_type+

Age_of_mother_at_first_birth+Wealth_index+Marital_status+Mother_occupation+Birth_type+Sex_of_child+BORD+Place_of_delivery+f(clus,model="iid")

model1=inla(formula,family="coxph",data=mydata,verbose=T,control.hazard=list(model="rw1",n.intervals=20),debug=FALSE,control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,waic=TRUE))

summary(model1)

formula1=inla.surv(time,Status)~Region+Residence+Mother_education+Source_of_water+Family_size+Toilet_type+Age_of_mother_at_first_birth+Wealth_index+Marital_status+Mother_occupation+Birth_type+Sex_of_child+BORD+Place_of_delivery+f(clus,model="iid",hyper=list(prec=list(param=c(0.001,0.001))))

model2=inla(formula1,family="weibullsurv",data=mydata,verbose=TRUE,control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,waic=TRUE))

summary(model2)
